details:
### Impact

Gradle runs work — compilation, tests, and Worker API actions — in forked **worker** processes that communicate with the long-lived **Gradle daemon**. The worker ↔ daemon socket is a loopback TCP connection that performs no authentication of the connecting peer. The connection is accepted on a first-come basis during a short window while a worker starts. Each message on that channel can be encoded with a per-type serializer but uses Java serialization as a fallback. This advisory is about a vulnerability on this communication channel. 

An attacker who can place bytes on this channel can cause the daemon to deserialize a hostile object graph which can lead to **remote code execution in the daemon JVM** or a **denial of service** (a crash or resource exhaustion from a malformed or deeply nested graph). This has been demonstrated with a proof-of-concept. Code execution in the daemon runs with the privileges of the user running the build and exposes in-memory and on-disk secrets available to it. This advisory does not publish the proof-of-concept.

Builds running on **shared / multi-user build hosts** are the most at risk. The vulnerability requires an actively running Gradle build and requires the attacker to win a race to connect during the short window between a worker process starting and the daemon accepting a connection from it. 

This vulnerability is not exploitable from a remote network connection.

### Patches

Gradle has updated the worker/daemon protocol to use a per-connection secret for authentication.

| Fix version | Availability |
| ---------- | ----------- |
| 9.8.1 | OSS |
| 9.7.2 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) |
| 9.6.2 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) |

### Workarounds

Upgrading Gradle is our recommended fix. 

If you cannot upgrade immediately:

* **Do not run builds on shared, multi-user machines.** Ensure only trusted users have local (same-host) access to a machine while a Gradle build/daemon is running. On CI, prefer single-tenant, ephemeral runners rather than shared hosts. The attacker must be a co-located local principal to gain access to the Gradle build.

If you cannot apply these mitigations, restrict which users and processes share a host with your builds until you can upgrade.

### Forensics

When a message not originating from the worker takes over the connection, the worker process will fail its connection attempt and Gradle will report this error in the build output:

```
org.gradle.internal.remote.internal.ConnectException: Could not connect to server [<id> port:<port>, addresses:[/127.0.0.1]]. Tried addresses: [/127.0.0.1].
	at org.gradle.process.internal.worker.child.SystemApplicationClassLoaderWorker.call(SystemApplicationClassLoaderWorker.java:…)
	…
	at worker.org.gradle.process.internal.worker.GradleWorkerMain.main(GradleWorkerMain.java:…)
Caused by: java.net.ConnectException: Connection refused
```
This error will then be reported as a failure of the task or operation that started the worker.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> The lack of a log entry cannot be used to conclude no such attack was performed. The presence of a log entry is not a confirmation that an attack happened, but an indication that more investigations are needed.

### References

*[ Gradle architecture standard ADR-0002,](https://github.com/gradle/gradle/blob/master/architecture/standards/0002-avoid-using-java-serialization.md) "Avoid using Java serialization" — Gradle's own guidance to move off Java serialization, citing deserialization security among the reasons.
* [JEP 290: Filter Incoming Serialization Data](https://openjdk.org/jeps/290)
* [Deserialization of untrusted Java objects before authentication in the client - daemon communication](https://github.com/gradle/gradle/security/advisories/GHSA-xwqc-3h47-hg64)
